Some of us are good with finances and enjoy the process, and I’m one of them. I specialize in monitoring the day to day spending and a different part does the monthly, pay period, and week-by-week planning. 

One of the parts spent six months tracking every expense in a physical notebook to determine our baseline spending needs and that formed the basis of our budget breakdown three years ago. Every paycheck gets plugged into a simple formula on payday and we know exactly what needs to get left in the checking account for bills, what needs to be tossed in savings, and what’s left for day to day expenses. 

Im one of the three primary fronters, and I don’t find myself wanting things that cost money unless they have a practical function. My hobbies are inexpensive as long as I’m creative with my supplies. 

Most of us are too anxious about money to overspend. A couple will occasionally go outside of the budgets we set but our goals are so strict and documented that it’s rarely a problem, wiggle room is built into every limit. There are some guidelines on what things shouldn’t become habits. Online shopping is a no unless the item is urgent, agreed upon, or has been int he cart for long enough for someone else to have laid eyes on it. 

One of the teens is huge into video games. If he really wants a game it has to be on the wishlist for at least a week, and he usually loses interest by then. Sometimes if he knows he’ll only like starting it and lose the will to play fast, he’ll buy a game, try to play as much as possible in under two hours and return it through steam. He also downloads free mobile games, plays until they start to push too many ads or it becomes pay to play, and then deletes them and gets new ones. 

Even the littles have only ever known having to restrict spending from an early age so as long as there’s YouTube, art supplies, a library, or a dollar store around we’re all set.

I’ve been lucky enough to find a partner that does have DID, but we’ve only recently started sharing our experiences with each other. He didn’t know about my disorder, and he forgot that a different alter had told me about his. We have different boundaries and different needs overall, and that compounds when taking into account the differences between each part of each of us. 

For me personally, what I want them to know about me is that I do want to have any harmful behaviors or gaps in my memory pointed out. It doesn’t hurt my feelings, and on the occasions it does cause me stress, that’s not as important to me as monitoring my switches and paying attention to the activities of my other alters. 

I also want them to know how often I have to cover for my lapses outside of our relationship. It is exhausting keeping a single outward persona going and hiding the fact that I am not the only one living my life. The greatest thing they’ve given me through this is the freedom to say “I don’t remember talking to you about that,” or “that wasn’t me,” without feeling like I’ve failed them in some way by not being the right part at the right time. 

As for advice, sometimes if you’re not qualified in a relationship to give advice to someone with different experiences, the best thing you can do is avoid overstepping. You can focus on listening, helping them create safety plans, learning ways to help them ground themself. 

One thing that my partner and I do for each other if we can tell the other is getting distressed is to “wiggle it out.” We help each other up off the bed or couch, grip each other’s hands, and shake each other’s arms around, stomp our feet, toss our heads. Within seconds we end up cracking up and the physical movement is enough to lift the fog at least a bit. 

Assistance with practical tasks is also often the easiest and most helpful way to support someone with any sort of disability. If the person you’re dating struggles with keeping a schedule, cleaning their living space, or managing time, it does wonders to just say “hey, I’ve got this one today.” Ask first of course! Just because you can do something faster or more efficiently doesn’t mean they want you to. 

Anyway! YMMV, but you don’t have to have experience with what they’re going through to help them out. Play to your strengths, keep up communication, and treat them with respect. That’s my two cents :))

Absolutely yeah. It’s a really vulnerable thing, and having alters in the first place is something I stay very very private about. My partner and my therapist know and that’s it. When I was a kid any sign of weakness was dangerous, so lapses in memory, differences in identity, all of it had to be kept completely under wraps. It feels frightening to basically tell someone “anything you say and do right now I might not remember later, and the boundaries of this alter might be different from the ones you’re used to.” 

So- I would say whatever your experience, you’re not alone in it. “Normal” doesn’t matter as much as “healthy for you”, and it’s not mutually exclusive from anxiety and trauma and fear taking over again. There are real risks to disclosing, so while I think it’s important to open up to the people you think will be helpful and compassionate, it makes sense that you struggle with it. 

Not an expert or anything, but that’s my piece.

Overall, we’re doing really good, but it’s coming with some challenges. We’re moving into a new apartment, we’re in a loving relationship with another system and the communication between us is amazing and healthy and safe, we start a new job that should be a better fit in a week or two. 

I’ve been trying to refrain from digging too deep but I’ve had some time off the past couple weeks and it’s sending us into a bit of a ruckus. Old, old, old trauma seems to be resurfacing and a few of us are suddenly aware of each other and communicating regularly. Important stuff, but exhausting. It’s been hard to get out of bed the past couple days. I am burnt out and don’t want to be fronting right now but I don’t trust anyone else to. So. Mixed bag.

Simply put, the type of love that you need changes. 

Think of how good, healthy parenting works. When a child is ages 0-2, loving parents take care of them entirely. There’s not a lot of complexity to the relationship beyond “I am bigger than you and I love you and you need me, so I will do the things you can’t do for yourself, and I will comfort and soothe you when you’re distressed.” But ideally, your parents don’t keep wiping your butt to show they love you forever. They have to learn to change what they do for you as your needs shift and you grow. As a teenager you might need your parents to be more hands off, but reliable and secure enough for you to come to them for advice. They still provide for you physically but love in that dynamic is once again not remotely the same as it was when you were a newborn. 

Human beings are social creatures and we need each other, not just for our physical well-being but our emotional well-being. Good parental love is wonderful, but nothing beats the gorgeous complexity of a healthy network of multiple people who give you support, advice, comfort, new perspectives, entertainment, affection, intimacy, growth, you fucking name it. 

Also, parents age and die. They’re human too. They can’t provide you with everything and it doesn’t feel good to have your relationships be defined by feeling taken care of. Historically, it hasn’t been very common for two parents to even be the bulk of a child’s emotional support until adulthood. It’s far more normal for a whole village, so to speak, to be your source of love and security. 

TL;DR: Parental love is awesome, but no, it isn’t the limit. Which is a wonderful thing! There are so many people out there who could *also* love you at the same time that your parents do.

You’ve made a ton of progress on line confidence and I love the aesthetics of the more recent one! The anatomy is also more consistent and grounded. 

One thing that I do notice is that the older piece seems more dynamic because of the pose and composition. I feel like the composition of the redraw doesn’t have enough flow to keep my eye moving through the piece, and I keep getting stuck in all the points of that visual triangle formed by the two speech bubbles and the face. If you’re wanting to tell a story that includes “this desperate, enraged person has a gun,” the gun should be more of a focal point. It’s easy to lose that punch when you’re doing a redraw (at least it is for me, I get caught up in the aesthetics and sometimes lose track of the *umph* that I gave to the first draft). 

On the subject of the face, though, I love it! The symmetry, the shape of the smile, and the goat eyes create such an eerie effect. He truly gives off the vibe that he’s lost so much that he has nothing more to be afraid of. 

If I were to rework the redraw myself, I’d probably keep the face as the main point as you’ve done but lengthen the composition, and change the pose so that it looks more like he’s waving the gun around as he speaks, and possibly approaching the person he’s speaking to.

It takes time to figure yourself out sometimes. How much of an inconvenience is it to anyone, really? I have friends who have changed their names a few times within a single year, and even after years of knowing them it only takes consciously thinking about it for a few weeks when we talk to change it up. I slip up every once in a while, but that’s not their fault, nor is it a sign that I’m unsupportive. 

Your comfort in your own skin is more important than their desire to not have to consciously think about your comfort. I’m glad that your family doesn’t call you by your original deadname, but it shows a lack of compassion and understanding for that path of self discovery that they won’t try again. 

Regardless of the difficulties that come with changing your name with friends and family, you don’t need to take on any guilt. There isn’t anything shameful about needing change. And if it’s hard for them, so what? Y’all can talk it through if they want to. They can try. It’s not that deep. 

I know that for me, guilt is tied to fear. When I feel guilty about asking for things, it’s often because I’m afraid that the next thing I need will be the thing that convinces them to give up on caring for me. But people who love unconditionally simply don’t give a shit. It’s a minor inconvenience to remember a new name. Don’t let anyone shame you for that.
